newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia's Drnovsek forms centre-right cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia's Drnovsek forms centre-right cabinet.

text.p: Slovenia's prime minister -designate Janez Drnovsek said he had formed a new cabinet in coalition with the conservative People's Party and pensioners' party Desus.
"I hope this will be a foundation for a strong government for the next four years," Drnovsek told Radio Slovenia late on Monday.

Drnovsek, of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, who has been acting prime minister since April 1992, put the government line-up to parliament less than two hours before the deadline expired at midnight on Monday.
An inconclusive general election on November 10 had divided the parliament into even blocks of leftwing and rightwing parties.
According to the cabinet proposal, the Liberal Democrats and the People's Party will each get nine ministerial posts, while Desus will have one minister.
The Liberal Democrats will take the posts of foreign minister, finance minister and interior minister, while the People's Party will get the defence, justice and agriculture portfolios.

Zoran Thaler will be the new foreign minister. Thaler, who held the same post for over a year until May 1996, was ousted by parliament, accused of blocking progress in Slovenia's association agreement with the European Union, which was signed in June 1996.
Mitja Gaspari, who has been finance minister for the past four years, will keep his post.

"I believe this was a healthy compromise that is positive for Slovenia. Within the posibilities given by a tight electoral result we reached the best solution," Marjan Podobnik, head of the People's Party, told the radio.
The new coalition has 49 of the 90 parliamentary seats but is also expected to have the support of two representatives of Hungarian and Italian minorities and an independent delegate.
Drnovsek's initial proposal for a leftist cabinet in coalition with former communists the United List of Social Democrats was rejected 12 days ago by an even vote of 45 against 45.

The parliament is expected to vote on the new cabinet between Tuesday and Thursday next week. If it fails to approve at least two thirds of the line-up, president Milan Kucan will have to nominate a new prime minister.
The new government will be the third since Slovenia's independence from the former Yugoslavia in 1991.
